title: Maha Shivaratri: the great night of Shiva
hook: a night kept awake, water poured over the lingam, Om Namah Shivaya until dawn
tomorrow: Raksha Bandhan: the thread of protection

segments.voice: Yesterday, Holi in Braj: Krishna coloring Radha's face so they'd match. Your line was everyone's the same color today. What did you find in common? Today, Shiva's night again, and a pillar with no end. Day ninety.

Two gods are having an argument. Brahma, the creator, says: I made everything, so I'm the greatest. Vishnu, the preserver, says: I hold everything together, so I am. It's an argument you could hear at any dinner table: who matters most. And it's getting heated. Then, between them, out of nowhere, a column of fire bursts up out of the ground. It rises past the clouds. It goes down past anything they can see. It has no top and no bottom. And both of them stop talking.
screen: `WHO IS THE GREATEST?` → `A COLUMN OF FIRE.` → `NO TOP, NO BOTTOM.`

segments.voice: This story is told in the Shiva Purana, and in others too. The two gods make a deal: whoever finds the end of the pillar wins. Vishnu becomes a boar and starts digging down. Brahma becomes a swan and flies up. They go for what the story calls ages. Vishnu digs and digs, and never reaches the bottom. He comes back and says, honestly: I couldn't find it. Brahma flies and flies, and never reaches the top. On the way he sees a flower drifting down, and in many tellings, he takes it back as proof and claims he found the top. He didn't. Then the pillar opens, and Shiva steps out of it. The light was him all along. In the tellings, Vishnu is honored for his honesty, and Brahma is rebuked for the lie. This is one of the stories people tell about the lingam, the rounded stone at the heart of a Shiva temple. Some understand it as a small image of that pillar of light: no beginning, no end. And some say this is the night it happened, the great night of Shiva. Others remember his wedding to Parvati, or his cosmic dance, on this night. Households hold these reasons side by side. Now look at what the story is doing. The argument was about who was biggest. The answer was something so big that neither of them could measure it. The only right response was to stop, and pay attention. Stay awake for what matters.
screen: `A BOAR DIGS, A SWAN FLIES.` · `NEITHER FINDS THE END.` · `THE PILLAR OPENS: SHIVA.` · `THE LINGAM, A PILLAR OF LIGHT.` · then, large: `STAY AWAKE FOR WHAT MATTERS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: three breaths longer than you want to. Sit, and let the breath come and go. Picture the pillar of light, rising above you and going down below you, farther than you can follow. You don't have to reach the end of it. Just stay with it. When the voice comes that says, that's enough, take three more breaths. No boar, no swan. Just staying. The bell holds the time.
Shivaratri. The great night of Shiva. For many, the night the pillar of light appeared, with no top and no bottom.
Your line: stay awake for what matters. Today, the next time an argument turns into who matters most, stop, and notice something bigger than both of you. Day ninety.

howItsDone: On Maha Shivaratri many Hindus fast, keep a night-long vigil in Shiva temples, pour water, milk and bilva leaves over the lingam, and chant Om Namah Shivaya; many temple carvings show Shiva appearing from the pillar of light.

original.note: Sanskrit: the emergence from the linga, the name for this story and its temple image.

trapdoor: what you thought: a night to honor Shiva.
what it means: for many, the night a pillar of light with no end silenced an argument about who was greatest.
what a scholar hears: the Lingodbhava story, told in the Shiva Purana and other Puranas, carved on the back wall of many South Indian Shiva temples.

sources.ref: Shiva Purana, Vidyeshvara Samhita (the pillar of fire, Brahma and Vishnu)

notes: Lingodbhava: in the Shiva Purana (Vidyeshvara Samhita) the flower is the ketaki, which lies with Brahma; Vishnu is honored. The Shiva Purana links this appearance to Shivaratri. Confirm citations and details; the ketaki is not named in the script.
Brahma's punishment varies (loss of worship, a head cut by Bhairava); the script says only 'rebuked'. Confirm.
Lingam described as 'many understand it as a small image of that pillar of light'; a Keeper should check this framing among other meanings.
Lingodbhava panels on the rear (west) wall of the sanctum in many Tamil Shiva temples. Confirm.
Original: लिङ्गोद्भव (Lingodbhava). Confirm spelling and pronunciation.
